name: Rhinoplasty simulation apps

card.summary: Morphing and 3D-imaging tools that preview how a nose might look after surgery; used by clinics and by prospective patients, with outcomes that are not guaranteed.
card.note: A simulated preview is an illustration, not a promise of surgical result.

quick.overview:
Rhinoplasty simulation software lets a person or a surgeon alter a photo or 3D scan of a nose to show a proposed change. Clinics use 3D cameras and planning platforms such as Vectra and Crisalix during consultations, and consumer apps offer similar photo morphing.

The appearance payoff is a preview: people can see a candidate profile or tip before surgery and explain to a surgeon what they want. Studies in clinics report that patients find 3D previews useful and that how closely a simulation resembles the result tracks with satisfaction.
quick.how: The surgeon or clinic takes photographs from several angles or a 3D camera capture, and software merges them into a 3D model of the face. The operator reshapes the nose digitally, often showing options side by side, and the patient rotates the model to review it. The process in one published clinic study took 10 to 15 minutes. Some platforms let patients view the simulation from home.
quick.risks: The tools themselves are low-risk. The surgical result can differ from a simulation: one study found the simulation slightly overestimated tip projection, and the authors state that simulations do not guarantee results. Healing and swelling vary between people, and swelling can take a year or more to fully settle.

lead: Rhinoplasty simulation apps and software let people preview how a nose might look after surgery by editing a photo or a 3D model of their own face. The aim is to see a proposed profile, tip or bridge before committing, and to give surgeon and patient a shared picture of the target [1][2].

In clinics, the preview is usually built from three photographs taken from different angles, merged into a 3D image, or from a 3D camera capture, and the surgeon then reshapes the nose on screen [2]. Cloud platforms such as Crisalix generate 3D previews from 2D photos or scans and can show treatment options side by side [3]. Consumer apps offer simpler photo morphing.

Published studies have looked at how patients and surgeons perceive these tools and at how closely simulations match results. In a Japanese clinic series, similarity between the simulation and the result correlated with postoperative satisfaction, and a 172-patient series found that most patients felt 3D added value over 2D previews [2][4].

angle.text: A preview helps a person decide what change to ask for, see whether it suits the rest of the face, and communicate it to a surgeon. Previews are visual predictions and are not a guarantee of the surgical outcome.

paras: Rhinoplasty references describe software-based 3D simulation as a way to show existing deformities and plan the proposed approach, and 3D cameras as a way to inspect and edit the nose virtually so that both parties can discuss a likely outcome [1]. Pre-operative consultation also includes a history, an exam of skin type, symmetry, valves and septum, and photographs from several angles, which supply the images these tools work from [1].

In a Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open series, a handheld Vectra H1 system took three photographs from different angles and merged them into a 3D image, and a morphed image reflecting the patient's anatomy and aesthetic ideals was produced in roughly 10 to 15 minutes [2]. Crisalix describes a web platform that uses artificial intelligence and cloud technology to create 3D previews from 2D photos or scans and to compare options side by side, with remote viewing for patients [3]. One clinic's description of the Vectra face sculptor says viewers can zoom, rotate the model and compare scenarios such as a nose with and without a chin implant [6].

Healing differs between people and swelling can take at least a year to fully diminish, which affects how closely a preview resembles a final result [1]. Wikipedia reports revision surgery in roughly 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties [1].

Computer-assisted surgical simulation more broadly uses specialised software to render a patient's data as a virtual 3D model and simulate the intervention beforehand, with maxillofacial examples such as navigation in orthognathic surgery [5].

A retrospective single-centre study in Japan of 38 aesthetic rhinoplasty patients who viewed Crisalix 3D simulations used the FACE-Q rhinoplasty module. Similarity between the simulation and the result correlated with satisfaction with the nose (rho 0.66), while surgeon aesthetic scores correlated somewhat more strongly (rho 0.71). The simulation overestimated nasal tip projection by about 0.7 mm and underestimated the nasofrontal angle by about 1.7 degrees; length, alar width and nasolabial angle did not differ significantly. Satisfaction rose from 39.0 to 74.8 after surgery. The authors note the small, retrospective design, follow-up of at least six months, an all-Asian sample, and that simulations do not guarantee results [4].

A 2019 series of 172 rhinoplasty patients compared 2D simulation with 3D morphing. 95 percent of patients said 3D added value over 2D, surgeons saw added value in 66 to 74 percent of patients, and revision patients reported better understanding of the surgical aims (84 percent) than primary patients (61 percent). The study measured perceptions and did not compare simulations with postoperative results [2].

timeline.event: A 172-patient series reports patient and surgeon views of Vectra 3D morphing versus 2D simulation in rhinoplasty consultation [2].
A Japanese series links Crisalix simulation accuracy to FACE-Q satisfaction after rhinoplasty [4].
